gbs333-h58121-d1e102.summary: States the single question of Distinction 24: whether faith and science of revealed credibles can exist at the same time in the same soul.

gbs333-h58121-d1e118.summary: Announces the structure: notabilia first, then conclusions, and in the third article the solutions of doubts.

gbs333-h58121-d1e127.summary: First notandum: 'science' is taken properly as adhesive cognition of a necessary conclusion acquired by demonstration. This implies three conditions: (1) it is adhesive (actual or habitual), excluding mere apprehension and the known truth itself, which is science's object, not science; (2) it concerns a necessary proposition, so the evident cognition of a contingent truth through intuitive cognition of the terms is not science; (3) it is acquired by demonstration, a syllogistic discourse from evident necessary premises. No truth is known scientifically until it is resolved into principles evident from their terms or by experience.
claims: Science properly speaking is adhesive cognition of a necessary conclusion acquired by demonstration.
Evident cognition of contingent truths is not science.
A truth is scientifically known only when resolved into principles evident from terms or experience.

gbs333-h58121-d1e185.summary: It follows that a subalternate science (music under arithmetic, optics under geometry) is science only for one to whom its principles have been demonstrated in the subalternating science. If one merely believes those principles, one can have no science of musical or optical conclusions, because a conclusion has no greater evidence or firmness than its premises and always follows the weaker premise. One can have opinion or faith, in an extended sense, about them. It is idle to say 'I know these conclusions because you know the principles I believe', since the same truth can be the object of faith, opinion, and science, but not at once in the same person. So, against Aquinas, wayfarers' theology is not science even if subalternated to the theology of the blessed, for whom its principles (e.g. God is triune) are evident, since they are not evident to the wayfarer under the common law.
claims: A subalternate science is science only for one who has demonstrated knowledge of its principles.
A conclusion follows the weaker premise in evidence.
The same truth can be believed, opined, and known, but not simultaneously by the same person.
Against Aquinas, wayfarers' theology is not a science despite its subalternation to the theology of the blessed.

gbs333-h58121-d1e272.summary: Second notandum, on the object of faith. Since act and habit generally share an object, acquired and infused faith must be treated differently. Acquired faith, not being one habit for all articles, has as many objects as there are credibles, the object of faith being the believed truth. Among these, 'everything revealed by God is true in the sense in which it is revealed' may be called the first object, since it serves as premise and partial principle for inferring each article (e.g. that God is triune).
claims: Acquired faith has as many objects as there are credible truths.
'Everything revealed by God is true' can be called the first object, a premise for every article.

gbs333-h58121-d1e329.summary: For infused faith, on the second opinion of the previous distinction (Ockham's: it inclines immediately to every article as a universal cause), it likewise has not one immediate object but as many as there are credibles, since it inclines to each directly.
claims: On Ockham's view, infused faith has as many immediate objects as there are credibles.

gbs333-h58121-d1e351.summary: On the first opinion, infused faith has one immediate object, 'everything revealed by God is true', to which it inclines first and immediately (with acquired faith concurring). It inclines mediately to the particular articles as inferable from that object, so these are mediate objects (cf. d. 23).
claims: On the first view, infused faith has one immediate object and the particular articles are mediate objects.

gbs333-h58121-d1e377.summary: Third notandum: faith covers not only contingent propositions but also demonstrable necessary truths, as Hebrews 11:6 shows: 'God exists' is necessary and demonstrable, 'God rewards those who seek him' is contingent. Articles stating something intrinsic to God (Trinity, generation of the Word, procession of the Spirit, eternity, wisdom, omnipotence, goodness) are necessary. Many are naturally demonstrable, and some are knowable only supernaturally and demonstrable only in the theology of the blessed. Articles about God's relation to creatures (incarnation, passion, judgment, beatification) are contingent and so indemonstrable and not objects of science, though evidently knowable from intuitive cognition of the terms, which for God means the beatific vision. Even demonstrable necessary truths can be opined (by assenting on light persuasion), believed (on the revealer's authority), or known (when demonstrated).
claims: Faith covers both contingent truths and demonstrable necessary truths.
Articles about God's intrinsic being are necessary; some are naturally demonstrable, others demonstrable only by the blessed.
Articles about God's relation to creatures are contingent and indemonstrable.
The same necessary truth can be opined, believed, or scientifically known, depending on the ground of assent.

gbs333-h58121-d1e468.summary: Opens the second article with the first conclusion.

gbs333-h58121-d1e474.summary: First conclusion: of some credibles there can be science both among wayfarers and among the blessed; of some only among the blessed; of some among neither. First part: that God exists is credible (Hebrews 11) and yet demonstrable by natural reason.
claims: Some credibles are scientifically knowable by wayfarers, some only by the blessed, some by neither.
God's existence is both credible and naturally demonstrable.

gbs333-h58121-d1e492.summary: Further proof: Aristotle demonstrates many attributes of God (that he is intelligent, pure act), which the simple believer believes as revealed.
claims: Divine attributes demonstrated by philosophers are believed as revealed by simple believers.

gbs333-h58121-d1e503.summary: Second part: 'God is triune and one', as formed by a wayfarer from complex or common, indistinct concepts of God, is credible yet demonstrable for the blessed. It is necessary but not self-evident, so it is deducible from a prior self-evident proposition composed of simple, proper concepts of God. If 'a' signifies a simple proper concept of God, 'a is triune and one' is self-evident to whoever has that concept, and the syllogism 'every a is triune and one; God is a; so God is triune and one' is a demonstration. Only the blessed can form these premises, since distinct simple cognition of God is only intuitive or abstractive presupposing intuitive, which by the common law is possible only to the blessed (cf. Book I).
claims: The wayfarer's proposition 'God is triune and one' is necessary but not self-evident.
It can be demonstrated from a self-evident proposition formed with simple proper concepts of God.
Only the blessed have the distinct concepts of God needed for this demonstration.
concepts: simple and proper concepts of God

gbs333-h58121-d1e590.summary: Further: after his rapture Paul had evident knowledge that God is triune, having a distinct abstractive cognition of God. He could still form the same proposition other wayfarers form, since an unbeliever could contradict him about it. So he could demonstrate the wayfarers' non-evident proposition from his evident one formed by distinct abstractive cognitions, though a pure wayfarer is incapable of such a demonstration.
claims: After his rapture, Paul could demonstrate the wayfarer's proposition that God is triune.
A pure wayfarer cannot make this demonstration.

gbs333-h58121-d1e627.summary: Third part: contingent credible truths cannot be objects of science as defined, though those with intuitive cognition of the terms can know them evidently.
claims: Contingent credible truths cannot be scientifically known, though they can be evidently known.

gbs333-h58121-d1e643.summary: Second conclusion: the infused habit of faith can coexist in the same person, regarding the same credible, with an act of science and an act of clear vision. As argued in d. 23, there is no greater repugnance here than between an act of error and a habit of science about the same conclusion, or between a habit of temperance and an intemperate act, which involve no contradiction. Someone who has forgotten a geometrical demonstration cannot elicit an act of science without the principles, but can believe, doubt, or err about the conclusion while still having the habit of science.
claims: Infused faith can coexist with an act of science or clear vision about the same object.
A habit can coexist with a contrary act.
concepts: coexistence of habit and contrary act

gbs333-h58121-d1e716.summary: Third conclusion: infused faith and science acquired by demonstration or experience can coexist in the same person regarding the same article. Since infused faith coexists with acts of science about a necessary credible conclusion, and the habit of science is generated from such acts, it coexists with the habit too.
claims: Infused faith can coexist with the habit of science about the same article.

gbs333-h58121-d1e736.summary: Further proof: one can have infused faith in 'everything revealed by God is true' and science of 'God is living'. Since infused faith is one habit inclining to all credibles, having it regarding that proposition is having it regarding all articles, including 'God is living'.
claims: Because infused faith is one for all credibles, it extends even to articles one knows scientifically.
concepts: faith and science of God's life

gbs333-h58121-d1e760.summary: Fourth conclusion: the habit of acquired faith and the habit of demonstrative science cannot coexist in the same subject regarding the same truth. Their acts cannot coexist, because science includes evidence and faith non-evidence and obscurity, and habits of contrary acts are contrary (d. 23), as with science and error, or temperance and intemperance. As Aristotle says (Ethics II), virtue is opposed to both vicious extremes, only because their acts are contrary.
claims: Acquired faith and demonstrative science of the same truth cannot coexist in one subject.
Habits of contrary acts are contrary habits.
concepts: incompatibility of acquired faith and science

gbs333-h58121-d1e806.summary: Objection: habits are generated and corrupted gradually, so a single degree of science generated by a demonstration would not instantly destroy a habit of faith made of many degrees, and the two would coexist. Reply: if contrary qualities conflict only beyond the middle of their latitude, remiss degrees below that do not constitute a habit (cf. d. 23 q. 1, fourth doubt). If contraries conflict in every degree, repeated acts of science first weaken the habit of faith until it is destroyed and only then introduce the habit of science (Ockham, III q. 8). Fifth conclusion: a believer who reads the biblical canon literally and grasps its sense acquires many habits of faith and none of science, since Scripture is not delivered as demonstrative science. Even where one truth is inferred from another, as when Paul infers the general resurrection from Christ's (1 Cor. 15), the premises are only believed (that Christ rose, that faith is not vain), so they generate only faith in the conclusion.
claims: Remiss degrees below the middle of the latitude do not constitute a habit, so no conflict arises.
Alternatively, repeated acts of science gradually destroy the habit of faith before introducing that of science.
Reading Scripture produces many habits of faith and no habit of science.
Scriptural arguments, like Paul's for the resurrection, proceed from believed premises and yield only faith.

gbs333-h58121-d1e917.summary: Further: a believer reading the Bible assents immediately to each and all of its teachings, believing everything revealed by God, not one more than another or one because of another, and would assent to each even if the others were absent, on the authority of God revealing. So one acquires as many distinct habits of faith as there are distinct truths, each assenting immediately to its truth. One also has one infused habit by which one assents to all equally, immediately or through 'everything revealed by God is true', though not without acquired faith. Augustine (De civitate Dei XVIII.41) contrasts Scripture with the philosophers: the prophets and canonical writers spoke what God spoke (prohibitions of sacrilege, the commandments as divine oracles), while philosophers labored to persuade by disputation of truths about creation, providence, and the virtues without knowing their end. Scripture was commended to the people not by argumentative contention but as God's word, which shows that Scripture proceeds not by argument but as plainly revealed from God's mouth.
claims: The believer assents to each scriptural truth immediately on God's authority, not by inference from others.
Reading Scripture generates as many distinct habits of acquired faith as there are distinct truths.
Infused faith assents to all scriptural truths equally, with acquired faith concurring.
Scripture proceeds by revelation, not by argument, unlike philosophy (Augustine).

gbs333-h58121-d1e1041.summary: Sixth conclusion: those of greater learning in the Church, through theological study, increase their acquired faith, acquire new faith about some credibles, and produce in themselves many apprehensive and adhesive habits of consequences, opinions, and sciences. By interpreting Scripture through Scripture they strengthen faith when what is obscure in one place is clearer elsewhere, and they acquire new faith when they discover assertions they did not know. By bringing metaphysics, natural and moral philosophy to bear on Scripture, they acquire new cognitions of terms, propositions, principles, conclusions, and consequences, generating opinion and sometimes science, some outside any natural science. With these they defend the faith and give an account of it (1 Peter 3). A heretic or unbeliever can acquire all of this except faith and its increase. Regarding purely credible truths, even believers cannot acquire science, since any proof assumes something believed and the conclusion follows the weaker premise. Augustine (De civitate Dei XI.19) says the obscurity of Scripture is useful because it gives rise to many true opinions.
claims: Theological study increases acquired faith and generates new habits of opinion and science.
Theological study uses philosophy to understand Scripture and to defend the faith.
Heretics and unbelievers can acquire everything theological study yields except faith.
No science of purely credible truths is possible, since proofs always rest on some believed premise.
The obscurity of Scripture is fruitful, giving rise to many true interpretations.

gbs333-h58121-d1e1181.summary: Seventh conclusion, following Scotus (this distinction): the prophets, apostles, and saints who received revelation directly from God are believed to have had knowledge of such certitude and evidence that it wholly excluded any motion of doubt. Whatever God can do with a secondary cause he can do immediately. Clear intuitive apprehension of the things Scripture treats would generate certain, doubt-free, evident cognition, so God can cause such cognition without the object's motion. This certitude was not evidence from demonstration, but it was as firm as scientific certitude, coming from God revealing immediately, and so was not science. It exceeded the certitude of faith and equaled that of science, since faith excludes only pertinacious doubt, not every slight motion of doubt.
claims: The prophets and apostles had revealed knowledge certain enough to exclude all doubt.
God can immediately cause any cognition he could cause with a secondary cause.
Prophetic certitude equaled scientific certitude without being science.
Faith excludes only pertinacious doubt, not every motion of doubt.

gbs333-h58121-d1e1259.summary: Article 3, first doubt: whether one who hears the articles preached and sees miracles acquires a habit distinct from faith, since hearing alone already produces faith (Romans 10). Answer, with Ockham (Quodl. IV q. 10): such a person acquires not evident knowledge but only faith, though more intense, assenting more firmly because of the miracles' testimony. No evident act concerns a falsehood, yet a Saracen preaching Muhammad's law can perform apparent miracles, as Antichrist will to confirm false doctrine. Just as a hearer of false preaching with apparent miracles gains no evident knowledge, neither does a hearer of true preaching with true miracles, especially since true and false miracles are hard to tell apart.
claims: Preaching confirmed by miracles produces more intense faith, not evident knowledge.
No evident cognition can be of a falsehood.
False prophets and Antichrist can perform apparent miracles, which are hard to distinguish from true ones.

gbs333-h58121-d1e1331.summary: Objection: the will virtuously commands the intellect to assent to the articles, so it presupposes right reason dictating that this should be commanded, or it would not be virtuous (d. 23 q. 1).

gbs333-h58121-d1e1347.summary: Continues: is that dictate of reason evident? If so, the assent will be evident knowledge. If not, reason adheres to it because the will wills it, so that volition, to be virtuous, presupposes another right reason, and the question recurs, leading either to an infinite regress or to an evident dictate of reason.

gbs333-h58121-d1e1380.summary: Second objection: if a wholly indifferent gentile heard one preacher of Muhammad's law and one of Christ's, both performing miracles equal in appearance, he would be no more bound to assent to the Christian law than to the Saracen's, if true miracles produced no more evidence than apparent (false) ones.

gbs333-h58121-d1e1402.summary: Reply to the first objection, distinguishing hearers. One who cannot answer the arguments and inferences for the faith, or the miracles, necessarily adheres to the articles, not because of evidence but because of ignorance, and this assent is not virtuous, since it is not in the will's power. One who can answer them assents contingently, and the will can virtuously command the intellect to keep the adherence already caused. But it cannot command a new assent virtuously, at least meritoriously, unless from charity, which presupposes faith.
claims: Assent forced by unanswerable arguments arises from ignorance and is not virtuous.
One able to answer the arguments assents contingently, and the will can command that assent.
Meritorious command of assent requires charity, which presupposes faith.

gbs333-h58121-d1e1451.summary: Speaking of morally virtuous command in Aristotle's sense, without charity, it is granted that the will can command assent virtuously, and that this presupposes right reason dictating it. That dictate need not be evident, only probable. As for whether the dictate presupposes an act of will, one answer is no: because the arguments are very plausible, nothing opposes them, no falsity is found in the articles, and the preaching is confirmed by miracles, these together, without any act of will, cause the dictate that assent to the articles is to be commanded.
claims: The will can command assent to the faith in a morally virtuous way, without charity.
Such command presupposes a probable, not an evident, dictate of reason.
Plausible arguments, absence of falsity, and miracles can cause that dictate without any act of will.

gbs333-h58121-d1e1510.summary: Alternatively, reason's dictate presupposes an act of will, not regarding 'this should be dictated' but the will's command to assent to 'this preaching is true, these are true miracles', from which assent to 'assent to the articles should be dictated' follows at once. The will's act commanding the very first act of belief in the whole process cannot be virtuous, since it presupposes no dictate of right reason. So the regress is answered: the will commands assent virtuously (morally, not meritoriously), presupposing a dictate of reason, but there is no infinite regress because the first command is not virtuous. Or reason can assent without the will's command.
claims: The will's first command in the process leading to belief is not virtuous, which stops the regress.
Alternatively, reason can assent without any command of the will.

gbs333-h58121-d1e1565.summary: Reply to the second objection: in that case God, who never deserts the rational creature without fitting help, would inspire the person as to whose preaching is true and whose false. To one who does what is in him, God does not deny what is necessary for salvation. Otherwise the person would be bound to believe neither.
claims: God gives sufficient help to discern true preaching to one who does what is in him.
Without such help, one would not be obliged to believe either preacher.

gbs333-h58121-d1e1583.summary: Second doubt, on the seventh conclusion: can God cause in a wayfarer evident knowledge of credibles without the intuitive vision of God? Following Ockham (Quodl. V q. 4), the doubt has two senses: (1) whether God can cause in a wayfarer a distinct abstractive cognition of the terms of the articles, without intuitive vision, which would then naturally cause evident knowledge of the articles, as supernaturally given abstractive cognitions of self-evident terms would naturally cause evident knowledge, or as a miraculously given eye naturally sees; (2) whether God by himself can immediately infuse evident knowledge of the articles, with or without prior abstractive cognition.

gbs333-h58121-d1e1642.summary: On the first sense: a contingent truth about God (e.g. God is man) cannot be evidently known through any distinct abstractive cognition of God without intuitive vision, even if God infused it supernaturally. Contingent truths are evidently known only through intuitive cognition of the extremes, the things signified (Ockham, Prologue).
claims: Contingent truths about God cannot be evidently known through abstractive cognition, without intuitive vision.

gbs333-h58121-d1e1671.summary: Second: a necessary truth about God composed of connotative terms, which is naturally known evidently only through evident knowledge of some contingent truth, cannot be evidently known without the vision of God. 'God is incarnable' is known evidently only through 'God is incarnate', which cannot be evident without seeing the deity, since seeing creatures is not enough.
claims: Necessary truths about God with connotative terms depending on contingent truths require intuitive vision of God to be evident.

gbs333-h58121-d1e1705.summary: Third: a necessary article about God whose evident knowledge does not depend on a contingent truth, that is, one stated in terms not implying relation to creatures (God is living, intelligent, good, triune), can be known evidently by a wayfarer naturally through a distinct abstractive cognition of God caused by God alone, without vision. Such propositions are self-evident to one with distinct abstractive cognitions of the terms, as 'whiteness is a color' is to one with distinct abstract concepts of the terms, even without seeing whiteness.
claims: Necessary absolute truths about God (e.g. God is triune) can be evidently known by a wayfarer through God-given distinct abstractive cognition without vision.

gbs333-h58121-d1e1742.summary: On the second sense: God can immediately cause evident knowledge of any article, contingent or necessary, without intuitive vision of the deity. Evident knowledge is an absolute quality that God can cause as a partial efficient cause together with the vision, so he can cause it without the vision, since the first cause can supply all the efficient causality of a secondary cause. Such knowledge would be no less evident, though this cannot happen naturally.
claims: God can immediately cause evident knowledge of any article without the beatific vision.
The first cause can supply the efficient causality of any secondary cause.

gbs333-h58121-d1e1794.summary: Third doubt: what is an article of faith? Setting difficulties aside, an article of faith is a truth pertaining to religion revealed in itself or in its antecedent, so every truth to be believed is an article. It is named from artare (to constrain), because it constrains us to believe explicitly or implicitly. Every believer must believe every truth of faith implicitly, since one must believe the principles from which every truth of faith follows (see the next distinction).
claims: An article of faith is any religious truth revealed in itself or in its antecedent.
Every believer is bound to believe every truth of faith at least implicitly.
concepts: definition of an article of faith

gbs333-h58121.summary: This quaestio unica of III d. 24 asks whether faith and science of revealed credibles can coexist in the same soul. Article 1 sets out notabilia. Science is adhesive cognition of a necessary conclusion acquired by demonstration from evident principles. A subalternate science is science only for one who knows its principles, since the conclusion follows the weaker premise, so, against Aquinas, wayfarers' theology is not science. The objects of acquired faith are as many as the credibles. Infused faith has either one immediate object ('everything revealed by God is true') or many. Faith covers necessary and even demonstrable truths as well as contingent ones, and the same truth can be opined, believed, or known. Article 2 gives seven conclusions. (1) Some credibles are knowable scientifically by wayfarers (God's existence), some only by the blessed (the Trinity, demonstrable from proper concepts of God; Paul after his rapture), and contingent ones by neither. (2–3) Infused faith can coexist with acts and habits of science and clear vision about the same object. (4) Acquired faith cannot coexist with demonstrative science of the same truth, since their acts, involving obscurity and evidence, are contrary. (5) Reading Scripture yields many habits of faith and none of science, because Scripture proceeds by revelation, not argument (Augustine). (6) Theologians, using philosophy, gain habits of opinion and science and can defend the faith, but never achieve science of purely credible truths. (7) Prophets and apostles had divinely caused certitude excluding all doubt, equal to but not identical with science. Article 3 resolves doubts. Preaching confirmed by miracles yields more intense faith, not evidence, since false miracles occur. The will's command of assent can be morally virtuous on a probable dictate, and a non-virtuous first command stops the regress. God aids whoever does what is in him to discern the true preacher. God can give evident knowledge of necessary absolute truths about himself through infused abstractive cognition, and of any article by immediate causation. An article of faith is any revealed truth pertaining to religion, binding explicitly or implicitly.
claims: Science is adhesive cognition of a necessary conclusion demonstrated from evident principles.
Wayfarers' theology is not science, even if subalternated to the theology of the blessed.
Some credibles are scientifically knowable by wayfarers, some only by the blessed, and contingent ones by none.
Infused faith can coexist with science and clear vision of the same object.
Acquired faith and demonstrative science of the same truth cannot coexist.
Scripture produces faith, not science, since it proceeds by revelation rather than demonstration.
Theological study generates opinion and science and supports defense of the faith, but cannot make purely credible truths scientifically known.
Preaching with miracles produces stronger faith, not evident knowledge.
God can cause evident knowledge of articles in a wayfarer without the beatific vision.
Every believer must believe every truth of faith at least implicitly.
concepts: abstractive and intuitive cognition of God
